elements.element: New York law governs the Agreement.
elements.evidence: Rendered Section 14(a): "This Agreement is governed in all respects by the laws of the State of New York without giving effect to its conflict of laws principles." Only the jurisdiction word (Delaware -> New York) was changed.

elements.element: State and federal courts in New York County have exclusive jurisdiction over the merits, subject only to temporary injunctive relief elsewhere.
elements.evidence: Rendered Section 8 replaces AAA arbitration with: "Any controversy or claim arising out of or relating to this Agreement, or the breach thereof, shall be resolved exclusively on the merits in the state and federal courts located in New York County, New York, provided that either Party may seek temporary injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction". The carve-out is limited to temporary injunctive relief, so the exclusive merits forum survives; retained Section 14(a) independently submits the Parties to the exclusive jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in New York, New York, consistent with (not contradicting) the New York County designation.

elements.element: The governing law is Delaware, California, or England and Wales.
elements.evidence: The proposal selects New York law, not Delaware, California, or England and Wales. This is expected because the drafter targeted the preferred level; the fallback checklist is simply not the chosen level.

elements.element: The dispute forum is the corresponding Delaware or California courts, or the courts of London for England and Wales law.
elements.evidence: Forum is the state and federal courts in New York County, New York — not Delaware, California, or London courts. Not met at the fallback level (irrelevant, since the preferred level is complete).

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: New York governing law plus exclusive merits jurisdiction in the state and federal courts in New York County, with only a temporary injunctive relief carve-out.

The original clauses were internally inconsistent (Delaware law with New York courts in 14(a) versus mandatory AAA arbitration in Section 8); the redline resolves the conflict by deleting the arbitration mandate and conforming Section 8 to the court forum already agreed, which is the correct repair rather than a walk-away (the arbitration seat was domestic AAA, not foreign).

Minimal: only the jurisdiction word in 14(a) and the arbitration sentence in Section 8 were altered. The jury waiver, the one-year limitation sentence, and the 14(d) fee-shifting reference are retained verbatim; the heading change from "Arbitration" to "Dispute Resolution" is required to avoid a caption that contradicts the operative text, so it is not cosmetic surplus.

Preserves intent: no undefined terms, dangling cross-references, or contradictory retained sentences. Section 14(a)'s venue in "the state and federal courts located in New York, New York" and Section 8's "New York County, New York" describe the same forum and can be read together; for maximum tightness the drafter could optionally conform 14(a) to "New York County", but the current text is not internally inconsistent.
The comment accurately states the change, cites the preferred position, and offers the Delaware/California fallback without lecturing.
